title: Central Texas Brisket
summary: Salt, pepper, post oak, and time. The cut that sorts out who actually runs a fire.
story: In Central Texas the meat is the sauce. A packer brisket gets a Dalmatian rub, a clean oak fire, and a long ride until a probe slides in like warm butter. Bark is the whole point. Wrap only after it is set — butcher paper, not foil — so the crust survives the stall. Then rest it like you mean it. Slice the flat against the grain, turn the point, and do not apologize for the fat.

items: 1 whole packer brisket, 12–16 lb, USDA Prime or high Choice
½ cup kosher salt (Diamond Crystal; use less if Morton)
1 Tbsp granulated garlic (optional — purists skip it)
Water or melted beef tallow for spritzing
Pink butcher paper for the wrap

steps.title: Trim like a butcher, not a sculptor
steps.body: Chill the brisket 30 minutes so the fat is firm. Knock off hard deckle fat, square ragged edges that will only burn, and leave about ¼ inch of fat cap. The point and flat meet at a seam — clean that up so heat can get in. Save trim for tallow.

steps.title: Dalmatian rub, edge to edge
steps.body: Mix salt and pepper 50/50 by volume. Coat every surface, including the sides. No mustard binder needed if the meat is slightly damp. Rest uncovered in the fridge 2–12 hours if you can; overnight dry brine pays off.

steps.title: Run a clean fire
steps.body: Hold 250–275°F with thin blue smoke. On an offset, feed splits before the fire starves — starving then flooding makes dirty smoke and bitter bark. Place the brisket fat-cap toward the cool side, thick end toward the firebox.

steps.title: Leave it alone until the bark is set
steps.body: No peeking for the first 3–4 hours. When the color is deep mahogany and the rub no longer rubs off on a wet finger, start a light spritz every 45–60 minutes to keep the surface from drying into leather.

steps.title: Wrap at the stall, not the clock
steps.body: Around 150–170°F internal the temperature stalls. Wrap in butcher paper only after the bark looks finished. Foil (the Texas crutch) speeds things up but steams the crust. Paper breathes.

steps.title: Probe, don't worship a number
steps.body: Start checking at 195°F. The flat is done when a probe slides in with almost no resistance in several spots — usually 200–204°F. The point can run hotter. If it still feels tight, give it more time.

steps.title: Rest longer than you think
steps.body: Hold unsliced in a dry cooler or a 150°F oven at least 1 hour, 2–4 if you can. Resting finishes the cook and lets juices settle. Slice the flat against the grain, about pencil-thick. The point grain runs a different direction — turn the knife.

proTips.text: Dirty smoke is a fire problem, not a wood problem. If the fire is gasping, you will taste it for 14 hours. Small splits, often, with flame always visible.
Injecting is a crutch for dry flats. A Prime packer, honest trim, and a real rest beat a syringe full of phosphates.
The grain in the point turns almost 90 degrees from the flat. Find it before you slice, not after you have a board of stringy beef.

milestones.label: Bark set
milestones.hint: Color is mahogany; rub no longer wipes off. Begin spritz.

milestones.label: Wrap window
milestones.hint: Stall, 150–170°F. Wrap only if bark is finished.

milestones.label: Probe tender
milestones.hint: Like warm butter in the flat. Usually 200–204°F.

milestones.label: Rest
milestones.hint: 1–4 hours unsliced. This is still cooking.

title: Kansas City Spare Ribs
finish: Bend test; meat pulls back ~¼ inch from the bone
summary: St. Louis–cut spares, a brown-sugar rub, and a sticky molasses glaze that is Kansas City in a bone.
story: Kansas City does not pick a lane. Beef, pork, chicken, and a sauce that is tomato, molasses, and smoke. Spare ribs — trimmed to a St. Louis cut — get a sweet-savory rub, a few hours of hickory, and a glaze in the last stretch so the sugar doesn't scorch. Tender, not falling off the bone. If they collapse into mush, you steamed them.

items: 2 racks spare ribs, St. Louis cut
Yellow mustard or hot sauce, as a binder

steps.title: Peel the membrane
steps.body: On the bone side, loosen the silver skin with a butter knife and pull it off with a paper towel. If you leave it, the rub never gets through and the bite is leathery.

steps.title: Rub and rest
steps.body: Thin coat of mustard, then the rub on both sides — heavier on the meat side. Rest at room temp 30 minutes while the pit comes to 250–275°F.

steps.title: Smoke bone-side down
steps.body: Run hickory with a little apple for sweetness. Spritz with apple juice after the first 90 minutes if the surface looks dry. Do not wrap unless you are in a hurry — unwrapped ribs keep better bark.

steps.title: The 3-2-1 myth
steps.body: Classic 3-2-1 (smoke, foil, glaze) is for people who like boiled ribs. For St. Louis spares, think 4–5 hours unwrapped, then a short glaze. Foil only if they are stalling hard and dinner is waiting.

steps.title: Glaze late
steps.body: Warm the sauce with vinegar and butter. Brush a thin coat in the last 20–30 minutes. Sugar burns; shine comes from thin layers, not a puddle.

steps.title: Bend, don't shred
steps.body: Pick up the rack with tongs in the center. It should bend into a U and crack on the surface, not break in half. Meat retracts about ¼ inch from the bone. Rest 10 minutes, slice between bones.

proTips.text: Sauce is a finishing coat, not a marinade. If you need a soup of it to make the ribs taste like something, the rub and fire didn't do their job.
Judges want a clean bite mark that shows smoke ring and moisture — not bones left naked in the box.

milestones.label: Color set
milestones.hint: Deep red-brown, about 2 hours. Spritz if dry.

milestones.label: Bend test
milestones.hint: U-shape with a surface crack. Rest 10 minutes.

title: Eastern Carolina Pulled Pork
summary: A whole pork shoulder, a vinegar-pepper mop, and no tomato in sight. This is the old eastern church-picnic cook.
story: Eastern North Carolina barbecue is chopped whole hog in its purest form. For a backyard pit, a bone-in Boston butt stands in and still tells the truth: salt, pepper, vinegar, crushed red pepper, and hickory. The sauce is thin enough to drink and sharp enough to cut the fat. Serve it on a cheap bun with vinegar slaw. Do not reach for ketchup.

steps.title: Season simply
steps.body: Salt, pepper, paprika over the whole shoulder. No heavy brown-sugar crust — eastern sauce is the seasoning. Overnight in the fridge if you have time.

steps.title: Fat cap up, long smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250–275°F, hickory or oak. Place fat cap up so it bastes as it renders. Expect 1½ hours per pound as a rough map, not a promise.

steps.title: Mop after the bark sets
steps.body: Whisk the vinegar sauce. After 4 hours, mop lightly every hour. You want a tangy bark, not a steamed roast. Keep the lid closed between mops.

steps.title: The stall is a feature
steps.body: Shoulders stall hard around 160°F. Wrap in paper if you need to make a window; otherwise ride it out. The collagen is still converting.

steps.title: Bone wiggle, then rest
steps.body: The blade bone should twist free with almost no effort, usually around 203°F. Rest 1 hour. Pull with your hands or cleavers, discarding the unrendered grease and the bone.

steps.title: Sauce in the pan
steps.body: Chop or pull, then dress with more vinegar sauce while the meat is hot so it drinks it. Taste for salt and pepper. Serve with slaw on the side, not mixed in unless you are feeding a crowd that asked for it.

proTips.text: If your sauce coats a spoon, you have left the east. It should rattle in the bottle.
Mix bark and inside meat. All inside is bland; all bark is a salt bomb. The chop is the blend.

milestones.label: Through the stall
milestones.hint: Don't panic at 160°F. Wrap only if time is tight.

milestones.label: Bone wiggle
milestones.hint: Blade bone twists free. Rest 1 hour, then chop.

title: Memphis Dry Ribs
finish: Toothpick between bones with little resistance
summary: No wet sauce on the rack. A brick-red rub, hickory, and a final dusting so the spice is the crust.
story: Memphis will sell you wet ribs if you ask. The ones that made the city's name are dry: a paprika-forward rub, a hotter pit than the low-and-slow gospel, and sauce on the table if you need it. Baby backs are the usual cut. The finish is a second coat of rub so every bite starts with spice, not syrup.

items: A little oil or mustard as binder

steps.title: Membrane off, rub on
steps.body: Peel the membrane. Oil lightly, then coat with rub. Keep a few tablespoons aside for the finish. Rest 30–60 minutes.

steps.title: Hotter than you think
steps.body: Memphis pits often run closer to 275–300°F. Baby backs are lean; they don't need a 6-hour funeral. Hickory only — it is the city's wood.

steps.title: No wrap, no glaze
steps.body: Smoke 3½–4½ hours bone-side down. Spritz with a little apple cider vinegar if the rub looks powdery-dry. Do not sauce the rack.

steps.title: Dust and rest
steps.body: When a toothpick slides between bones with little push, pull them. Dust with the reserved rub while the surface is still tacky. Rest 10 minutes. Sauce on the side for the tourists.

proTips.text: The second rub is the move. Without it you just have smoked pork. With it you have a crust that smells like a spice house.
Baby backs overcook in a blink once they are close. Start probing at 3 hours and trust the toothpick, not the clock.

milestones.label: Tacky bark
milestones.hint: Rub has melted into a crust. Spritz only if dusty.

milestones.label: Finish dust
milestones.hint: Toothpick tender. Second rub, then rest.

title: Santa Maria Tri-Tip
summary: California's ranch-country answer to barbecue: oak coals, garlic-salt crust, salsa on the side, 90 minutes start to slice.
story: Santa Maria tri-tip is live-fire, not overnight smoke. The cut is a triangular bottom sirloin that California butchers made famous. Season with salt, garlic, and black pepper, grill over red oak, and serve with pinquito beans and a sharp salsa. It is the weeknight cook that still feels like a gathering.

items: 1 tri-tip roast, 2–3 lb, fat cap trimmed to ¼ inch
½ tsp dried parsley or rosemary (optional)

steps.title: Season and find the grain
steps.body: Mix salt, garlic, pepper. Coat the roast. Look at the grain now — tri-tip grain turns in the middle. You will slice two directions later.

steps.title: Build two zones
steps.body: Red oak coals or a hot charcoal bed with a cool side. Sear the tri-tip 3–4 minutes per side over direct heat until a crust forms.

steps.title: Finish indirect
steps.body: Move to the cool side, fat cap up, lid on. Cook to 125–130°F in the thickest part for medium-rare. Carryover will take it a few degrees more.

steps.title: Rest and split the grain
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes. Cut the roast in two where the grain changes, then slice each piece against the grain, ¼-inch slices. Spoon salsa over. Do not smother it.

proTips.text: If you treat tri-tip like brisket you will dry it out. This is a steak with a different shape. Oak and a hard sear, then get it off.
Pinquito beans belong on the plate. If you can't find them, small pink beans with a little bacon and chili powder get you close.

milestones.label: Hard sear
milestones.hint: Crust on all sides over oak coals.

milestones.label: Slice two ways
milestones.hint: Split at the grain change, then against the grain.
